records.research_topics: postwar modernism; studio; half acre; Alcoa; aluminum; trellis; post and beam; fountain; construction chronology; carport; address verified; lot 60; garden plan; unbuilt designs; design phases; 1957 plan; Alcoa chronology; 1956 proposal; 1957 drawings; 1959 construction; solar control; microclimate; screens; pavilion; aluminum fountain; mixed materials; historical condition; preservation; loss of aluminum garden; 1996 visit; Eckbo; master tree plan; 1953
records.research_summary: Josef van der Kar designed Eckbo’s own house, described as a 1953 house in the caption; half-acre lot, about two-thirds level, reached by a 150-foot rising driveway; 1,500-square-foot house and 800-square-foot studio under one sloping roof. Photo caption dates trellis and screens to 1955 and describes the aluminum structures as Alcoa demonstration structures. Simon dates the single-story post-and-beam house designed by Josef Van Der Kar to 1952; the garden became an ALCOA Forecast Garden. She dates an ALCOA commission to 1959 and describes an abstract open-flower fountain and perforated aluminum overhead structures. Treib dates construction of the van der Kar-designed Eckbo house to 1951 and occupancy to 1952. His description gives approximately 1,500 square feet of living space and an 800 square foot studio initially separated by an open carport, later enclosed. The reproduced 24 April 1952 garden plan explicitly labels lot 60, tract 15007,8942 Wonderland Park Avenue, Los Angeles 46, Mr and Mrs Garrett Eckbo. Address and lot were visually verified in the plan title. Treib distinguishes an ambitious April 1952 garden proposal, a more restrained circa 1954 plan, a signed 12 November 1957 plan and the later ALCOA project; he states that no initial scheme appears to have been executed in its entirety. Treib traces ALCOA project correspondence to 16 October 1956, earliest existing drawings to 30 May 1957, and an agreement to 4 March 1959 before construction. The opening photo caption describes the garden in late 1959 shortly after completion. The garden responded to heat gain on east/south house glazing with aluminum sunbreaks, privacy screens, a freestanding pavilion and an abstract flower-form fountain. Expanded metal created filtered light and varying transparency; wood remained in structural supports and benches. Treib describes renovation consultations in 1987 and 1989 and reports that almost nothing of the original Forecast Garden’s aluminum ensemble remained on his 1996 visit; concrete aggregate paths with ceramic insets and wooden pavilion posts survived. He characterizes the original Forecast Garden as having effectively disappeared before 1988.

evidence.claim: Robert Riley reviews Eckbo’s 1950 book as an integration of design professions with science, including climatology, geology and hydrology; describes design as a tool for democracy and healthy environments.
evidence.subject: Landscape for Living review

evidence.claim: Riley considers the book’s vocabulary of materials, earth/rock/water, plants, structural elements and space/people useful for design analysis, while criticizing its universalism and limited attention to history and cultural difference.
evidence.subject: Landscape for Living review

evidence.claim: Eckbo treats architecture and landscape as interdependent parts of a continuous environment. Landscape quality depends on the relationships among structures, open space and earth, rock, water and plants.
evidence.subject: Architecture and the Landscape

evidence.claim: Landscape design continues after construction through growth, change, maintenance and later adjustments.
evidence.subject: Architecture and the Landscape

evidence.claim: Visual and physical circulation connect buildings, sites and neighborhoods. Floor level, wall openings and topography shape indoor/outdoor relations; buildings also create distinct microclimates affecting planting.
evidence.subject: Architecture and the Landscape

evidence.claim: Eckbo describes Wonderland Park as a three-block section at the upper end of Wonderland Park Avenue. Clem Roark located a subdivided but undeveloped 67-lot tract after Community Homes Cooperative failed.
evidence.subject: Wonderland Park

evidence.claim: Development in 1951 cleared vegetation and terraced the land by cut and fill. Eckbo notes compacted fill conflicted with garden cultivation, and that fitting houses and roads into the existing hillside had been considered.
evidence.subject: Wonderland Park

limitations: Image-only pages were OCRed locally using ArcGIS Pro Tesseract. Low-confidence photo/plan/handwritten pages are flagged in sources and require visual confirmation; their unverified text was not asserted as a factual claim.
Only explicit modern addresses and the visually confirmed Eckbo lot title were recorded; no coordinate was inferred from these readings.
General theory is separate from property-specific evidence; master-plan participation does not prove a commissioned individual garden.
House date and ALCOA chronology differ among sources; retain conflicting attributions.
Project index dates are archival project dates and should not replace house construction dates.
Locations are parcel centroids, not measured building footprints. Unmatched/ambiguous addresses are retained in the table but omitted from the map.
Index records are student research, not independently verified permits. Source-specific conflicting attributions remain visible.
